items.title: Where to Find the World’s Best Soup
items.author: Holyn Thigpen
items.summary: 20,000 BC was a monumental year in history. Why? The first pot of soup was crafted in a cave in modern-day China. To create their savory broth, prehistoric
items.text:
20,000 BC was a monumental year in history. Why? The first pot of soup was crafted in a cave in modern-day China. To create their savory broth, prehistoric humans boiled animal bones and entrails in crude pits, then slurped their handiwork from some of the world’s earliest ceramic bowls.


Fast forward a few thousand years, and a verdict has been reached: Our ancient ancestors were onto something ... something delicious. Since this first boiling pot, humans have come up with all kinds of ways to make delicious, simmering broths, loading them full of tender meat, starches, vegetables, and herbs. From light and clear dishes with delicate flavors to chunky creations of the stew variety, there’s no wrong way to make or enjoy a bowl of soup. Just put a pot on the stove and let the spirit move you.


In honor of this most versatile and reliable of comfort foods, we’ve compiled our favorite places around the world to dig into a big bowl of soup. From a Russian restaurant hidden in a bathhouse to a New Orleans mainstay that fed the civil rights movement, these restaurants show that soup is universal—a dish that bridges divides and soothes the soul. Grab your biggest spoon and your bib (because, yes, there will be spillage); we’re going on a delicious journey.


1. Wattana Panich - Bangkok, Thailand


Can soup be eternal? Apparently so, as this Bangkok eatery has been tending to the same massive, boiling pot of neua tune (beef stew) for 50 years. Owner Nattapong Kaweenuntawong has cooked this famous “half-century-old soup” since he was a kid working under his father, keeping the secret blend of spices and herbs, stewed beef, raw beef slices, meatballs, tripe, and other organs perfectly balanced. The ancient practice Kaweenuntawong uses to keep the soup constantly simmering is called Hunter’s Stew, using the previous day’s leftover broth as the base of the following day’s soup.

This would be Bún Riêu Gánh, the passion project of local legend Mrs. Mai Thi Lien. 4. Fio D’Italia - San Francisco, California

Also on the menu is a zuppa di cavolo con formaggio, a cabbage, bread and cheese stew with bits of prosciutto; and pasta e fagioli, a soup with—you guessed it—pasta, cannellini beans, and prosciutto. You can also rest assured that a thick, crusty half loaf of sourdough French bread will be brought to your table, complete with flaky salt and extra virgin olive oil. Mamma mia!

5. Au Pied de Cochon - Paris, France


Au Pied de Cochon was once known for using all parts of the pig in its dishes, from marrow bones to kidneys to heads and the eponymous hooves (it was founded by a former butcher after all). Unlike most other versions of French onion soup, which use beef stock as a base, Au Pied’s uses chicken stock to honor its Les Halles roots. Back when the area was still Paris’s central fresh food market, the soup became a go-to meal for blue collar workers and night owls roaming the “belly of Paris.” And since Au Pied de Cochon is open almost 24 hours a day (8 a.m. to 5 a.m.), you can still eat this fine soup at almost all hours of the night. (It’s perhaps even more delicious after an evening out.)


6. Chankonabe Shinzan - Tokyo, Japan

This tiny, hole-in-the-wall shop serves up a mean bowl of chanko nabe, a soup that combines meat or fish with tofu, vegetables, glutinous rice, and broth. The dish has long been the favorite of sumo wrestlers for bulking up and fueling for a fight, and Chankonabe Shinzan was, in fact, founded by Shinzan Takeyasu, a retired sumo wrestler and soup-maker extraordinaire.

Shinzan’s restaurant serves chanko nabe with both salt and curry-based broths (though the curry varieties are the clear favorite among locals). If you need something to tide you over till your soup is ready, there are appetizers like wagyu beef topped with green onions, snow crab salad, and tebasaki, double-fried chicken wings in a sweet-savory soy glaze. Just make sure to save room for the main event!

7. Appu’s Cafe - Long Beach, California


The rich soups at this Indian-Mexican fusion cafe are just what the doctor ordered ... literally. Appu’s was opened by Dr. Vinod Venkataraman in his retirement after a long career spent extolling the virtues of gingery broths and lentil stews. Chef VR (as those in the know call him) abides by the mantra: “Healthy eating is a choice, eating healthy is a lifestyle,” meaning everything on Appu’s menu is nutrient-dense and guilt-free.

Whether you opt for the spicy, protein-filled garbanzo bean soup or the creamy, nutty spinach soup, you’re in for a flavor-packed, warm, and satisfying treat. Pro tip: Pair your soup with the Maharani burrito, filled with rice pilaf and lentils and served with a special secret sauce.


8. A Touch of European Cafe - Glendale, Arizona


This family-owned joint serves up “pure comfort food done right”: hearty Polish classics like goulash, kielbasa, stuffed cabbage, and—to top it all off—an extensive list of signature soups. There’s truly a soup for everyone here, with options ranging from New England clam chowder to potato horseradish to chilled garlic; cold buttermilk and beets to cream of asparagus and beef tripe. All of these signatures pair perfectly with the cafe’s dark rye bread and pierogis, which you can wash down with a caramel apple cider or iced tea.


You can even learn how to make A Touch of European’s soups yourself at one of their twice-annual cooking classes, led by chef and owner Waldemar Okul. Whether you grew up on Polish cuisine or know only the basics, you’ll walk away from the experience with a Rolodex of beloved recipes to make at home. Past classes have included dishes like caprese on apricot walnut bread, chilled avocado and dill soup and, for dessert, a puff pastry Napoleon.

9. Dooky Chase’s Restaurant - New Orleans, Louisiana


Established in 1939, this NOLA institution has fed everyone from President Barack Obama to Nat King Cole and Reverend Martin Luther King Jr. Though Edgar “Dooky” and Emily Chase first opened Dooky’s as a sandwich shop, it grew into an upscale celebration of Creole cuisine after Leah, the Chases’ daughter-in-law, took over the business in the ’50s. As part of this revamp, she featured work by local Black artists on the restaurants’ walls—the first time many of them had seen their works publicly displayed.


Leah also added regional favorites like shrimp clemenceau, chicken creole, and creole gumbo to Dooky Chase’s menu, the latter of which still draws crowds with its winning combination of crab, shrimp, veal, and smoked and hot sausage. The restaurant also serves its signature green gumbo in the days leading up to Easter (made with nine different cooked greens). It may not look especially delicious, but it sure does taste good.


10. Farren’s Bar - Malin Head, Ireland


Ireland’s northernmost pub has been in the Farren family for six generations, drawing in folks from across County Donegal with its delicious seafood chowder and buttery, homemade soda bread. It’s the perfect hearty meal after a hike along Malin Head’s rocky cliffs or a swim through the harbor (especially if you add a Guinness to your order). The pub also boasts a fun bit of “Star Wars” trivia, having been visited by Mark Hamill during the filming of “The Last Jedi,” and even has a Yoda mural on its exterior.

11. Caldo de Piedra - Tlalixtac de Cabrera, Mexico


This small outpost outside Oaxaca is named after its signature dish, a fish and shrimp soup that is a staple of the indigenous Chinantec community. Traditionally, men would cook the soup right on the riverbank, seasoning their freshly caught fish with onions, lime, cilantro, and chiles. Caldo de Piedra keeps this centuries-old tradition alive today, using the same kind of fire-heated rocks to flash-cook and tenderize the fish. In fact, so revered is this practice that owner César Gachupín had to seek permission from town elders before opening his restaurant.


In 2021, the state’s congress declared the dish an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Oaxaca for its “symbolic importance as one of the dishes that best reflects the culture and society of the Papaloapan region.” Though it has historically been made by men, the soup is seen as a gesture of gratitude toward the women, children, and elders of the community.


12. Rung Rueang - Bangkok, Thailand


The tom yum soup at this unassuming spot has gained a cult following amongst Bangkok foodies, with large chunks of spicy-sweet pork balanced out by hints of lemongrass, chile, and lime. While this is the standard version of the dish, Rung Rueang offers plenty of ways to customize, with different broth bases, noodle types, and toppings: sugar if you wish to temper the heat, or a dusting of chile flakes to crank it up. The soup is so life-altering that Rung Rueang has been awarded a Michelin Bib Gourmand designation every year since 2018 and often has a line that snakes down the block.


Arriving to the shop, you’ll notice that it is, in fact, divided into two sections—the result of a decades-long family feud. While both still serve the dishes under the same names, the “left-side” shop (the original) is widely considered the better of the two.

items.title: AO’s Favorite Unusual Sites to Spend a Night
items.author: Holyn Thigpen
items.summary: Where to stay is a pivotal part of any trip, sometimes just as important as the destination itself. The place you rest your head can dictate not just the
items.text:
Where to stay is a pivotal part of any trip, sometimes just as important as the destination itself. The place you rest your head can dictate not just the quality of sleep you get but the kinds of activities you choose, the people you meet, and the way you engage with the culture around you.


That’s especially true at these accommodations, which are anything but ordinary—combining thoughtful design with unique entertainment and access to nature. From a secluded forest cabin to a lively circus camp, these places run the gamut from serene oases to bustling community hubs, catering to travelers of all ages and persuasions.


1. Tubakuba 📍 Bergen, Norway


This rabbit-hole-esque cabin, designed by students at the Bergen School of Architecture in 2014, overlooks the city from its perch on a forested cliff. Parties of up to five people (though families with young children are prioritized) can book a one-night stay in the building, crawling through its bent-timber hole into a cozy, minimalist interior. It’s not the largest accommodation—just barely squeezing in its lofted sleeping areas and old-school wooden stove—but offers beautiful views from a full wall of windows. And the best part? It’s free!

2. Kakslauttanen Arctic Resort 📍 Saariselkä, Finland


In the heart of the Arctic Circle, guests at Kakslauttanen can book a glass igloo for dreamy nighttime views of the northern lights (at their brightest from late August through April). However, if you’d rather stay in more traditional accommodations, there are a variety of spacious houses and cabins equipped with saunas, fireplaces, private outdoor space, and plenty of warm beverages. For the best of both worlds, try one of the resort’s Kelo-Glass Igloos, log cabins that contain a single jutting igloo room.

3. Villa Cheminée 📍 Bouée, France


Translating to “Fireplace” or “Chimney Villa,” this tiny hotel sits atop a 50-foot-tall tower built to resemble the chimneys of a nearby thermal power plant (the largest in Europe). Guests climb up a tall staircase to the top, where a double bed, kitchen, fireplace, and garden await them. For those who don’t have time to spend the night, the tower is also open for free visits on Sunday afternoons.

4. Brown Bear Watching Hide 📍 Palasi, Estonia


Estonia’s Alutaguse National Park is a haven for brown bears, and this rustic hideaway allows you to watch them go about their day, up close and personal. The two cabins, or “hides,” are quite spartan but allow for prime bear viewing, with chairs that look out through covert windows and special hatches for guests to take photos from. If you’re lucky, from your wooden bunk you may even spot a rare wolf or lynx roaming through the forest.


5. Atlanta Glass Treehouse 📍 Atlanta, Georgia


In Atlanta’s sleepy Ormewood Park neighborhood, one house stands apart from its bungalow neighbors ... that is, if you can spot it. Tucked away into the tree branches is this two-floor home made from recycled glass, steel, and milled lumber, constructed over four years by architects Mary Clare DeReuil and Carlos Tardio. They use the top floor as a studio for their firm, Tardio Architecture, but rent out the lower level on Airbnb, where guests enjoy two light-flooded bedrooms, industrial design, and giant doors that open onto four outdoor terraces.

6. Rabbit Tree Hostel 📍 Gili Meno, Indonesia


On the tiny island of Gili Meno, this wacky hostel has long attracted the artistically inclined with its fantastical decor and maze-like structure. Each colorful room has a distinct theme, from Grandma’s Room to the Riddle Room to Bola Bola (a massive ball pit). Walking to your room might mean getting lost in a hall of secret doors, ending up on an outdoor walkway, or stumbling upon a sunken table that occasionally fills with water. The hostel also places great focus on building community, and guests can join in for swims with glowing plankton, boat excursions, and game nights.


7. Libušín a Maměnka 📍 Pustevny, Czechia


These whimsical buildings are the work of Czech architect Dušan Jurkovič, known as “the poet of timber” for his intricate woodwork inspired by Czech and Slavic folklore. This cozy hotel, opened in 1899, was his ode to the mountain traditions of Pustevny, decorated with motifs drawn from local legends and heroes. In its operations, too, the space embraces alpine culture, serving local Wallachian cuisine like zelňačka (cabbage soup) and hosting folk musicians and dance troupes.


8. Grand Circus Hotel 📍 Malmö, Sweden


If you’ve ever dreamed of running away to join the circus, look no further than this quirky wagon park on an abandoned railway lot. The wagons are, in fact, old tractor-trailers, rebuilt and painted to recall the bohemian energy of a traveling circus. Each caravan’s design is inspired by a specific member of the circus; walking through the lot, you’ll find The Clown, The Magician, The Lion Tamer, and more. Grand Circus also has space for guests to park their own vans and take part in a lively community, as the space frequently hosts events ranging from stand-up comedy shows to folklore festivals.


9. Big Idaho Potato Hotel 📍 Boise, Idaho


On 400 acres of farmland just outside Boise, this six-ton spud invites visitors to try out a life in the belly of their favorite food. The site was originally constructed for the Idaho Potato Commission’s 75th anniversary and toured the country for seven years before arriving here in 2019. Now, after some DIY design, it’s open to the public on Airbnb, offering a cozy getaway replete with old vinyl records and a spa-like bathroom. Guests may even be greeted by Dolly, the friendly cow who lives on the property.


10. Attrap'Rêves Bubble Hotel 📍 Allauch, France


“Living in a bubble” isn’t always a bad thing, as proven by this series of see-through cocoons on the southern coast of France. Though they’re tiny (each a mere 13 feet in diameter), these plastic pods give guests 360-degree views of the surrounding forest and the sense of complete immersion in nature. Telescopes in each room let you take in the dazzling starry sky each night, and you can even order a luxury dinner for delivery to your pod.

Estonia’s Alutaguse National Park is a haven for brown bears, and this rustic hideaway allows you to watch them go about their day, up close and personal. The two cabins, or “hides,” are quite spartan but allow for prime bear viewing, with chairs that look out through covert windows and special hatches for guests to take photos from. If you’re lucky, from your wooden bunk you may even spot a rare wolf or lynx roaming through the forest.
5. Atlanta Glass Treehouse 📍 Atlanta, Georgia

In Atlanta’s sleepy Ormewood Park neighborhood, one house stands apart from its bungalow neighbors ... that is, if you can spot it. Tucked away into the tree branches is this two-floor home made from recycled glass, steel, and milled lumber, constructed over four years by architects Mary Clare DeReuil and Carlos Tardio. They use the top floor as a studio for their firm, Tardio Architecture, but rent out the lower level on Airbnb, where guests enjoy two light-flooded bedrooms, industrial design, and giant doors that open onto four outdoor terraces.
6. Rabbit Tree Hostel 📍 Gili Meno, Indonesia

On the tiny island of Gili Meno, this wacky hostel has long attracted the artistically inclined with its fantastical decor and maze-like structure. Each colorful room has a distinct theme, from Grandma’s Room to the Riddle Room to Bola Bola (a massive ball pit). Walking to your room might mean getting lost in a hall of secret doors, ending up on an outdoor walkway, or stumbling upon a sunken table that occasionally fills with water. The hostel also places great focus on building community, and guests can join in for swims with glowing plankton, boat excursions, and game nights.
7. Libušín a Maměnka 📍 Pustevny, Czechia

These whimsical buildings are the work of Czech architect Dušan Jurkovič, known as “the poet of timber” for his intricate woodwork inspired by Czech and Slavic folklore. This cozy hotel, opened in 1899, was his ode to the mountain traditions of Pustevny, decorated with motifs drawn from local legends and heroes. In its operations, too, the space embraces alpine culture, serving local Wallachian cuisine like zelňačka (cabbage soup) and hosting folk musicians and dance troupes.
8. Grand Circus Hotel 📍 Malmö, Sweden

If you’ve ever dreamed of running away to join the circus, look no further than this quirky wagon park on an abandoned railway lot. The wagons are, in fact, old tractor-trailers, rebuilt and painted to recall the bohemian energy of a traveling circus. Each caravan’s design is inspired by a specific member of the circus; walking through the lot, you’ll find The Clown, The Magician, The Lion Tamer, and more. Grand Circus also has space for guests to park their own vans and take part in a lively community, as the space frequently hosts events ranging from stand-up comedy shows to folklore festivals.
9. Big Idaho Potato Hotel 📍 Boise, Idaho

On 400 acres of farmland just outside Boise, this six-ton spud invites visitors to try out a life in the belly of their favorite food. The site was originally constructed for the Idaho Potato Commission’s 75th anniversary and toured the country for seven years before arriving here in 2019. Now, after some DIY design, it’s open to the public on Airbnb, offering a cozy getaway replete with old vinyl records and a spa-like bathroom. Guests may even be greeted by Dolly, the friendly cow who lives on the property.
10. Attrap'Rêves Bubble Hotel 📍 Allauch, France

“Living in a bubble” isn’t always a bad thing, as proven by this series of see-through cocoons on the southern coast of France. Though they’re tiny (each a mere 13 feet in diameter), these plastic pods give guests 360-degree views of the surrounding forest and the sense of complete immersion in nature. Telescopes in each room let you take in the dazzling starry sky each night, and you can even order a luxury dinner for delivery to your pod.

items.title: An Autumn in Sun Valley Is Unlike Any Other
items.author: Holyn Thigpen
items.summary: Sun Valley is renowned for its winter ski slopes, drawing in thrill-seekers with its 3,400 vertical feet and over 2,500 acres of diverse, snowy terrain.
items.text:
Sun Valley is renowned for its winter ski slopes, drawing in thrill-seekers with its 3,400 vertical feet and over 2,500 acres of diverse, snowy terrain. Meanwhile, in summer, this pocket of Idaho comes alive with wildflowers, festivals, and. a slew of outdoor activities. But autumn, considered by locals to be the “secret season,” is full of wonders both cherished and unexpected. With its radiant aspens, crisp mornings, and mild afternoons, this season brings out the best of Sun Valley’s natural beauty (and it doesn’t hurt that there are fewer crowds).


Whether you’re looking for arts and culture outings, outdoor adventures, or just some much-needed R&R, Sun Valley has everything you need for an unforgettable fall vacation. Come for a weekend and you’ll want to stay all autumn long, as the region comes alive with local traditions and cozy comforts. So, what are you waiting for? Start planning your getaway today with our guide to Sun Valley’s can’t-miss fall activities.

Oktoberfest


Every September, Sun Valley’s Champions Meadow hosts Ketchum Oktoberfest, a weekend-long celebration of beer and bratwurst. The meadow, just north of town on Sun Valley Road, fills up with picnic blankets, lawn chairs, and cornhole boards for an annual fundraiser tournament.


You’ll also want to stick around for the much-anticipated stein-hoisting competition, wherein competitors must hold a full beer stein with a straight, outstretched arm for as long as possible. Drinks at the festival are served by the local Sawtooth Brewery and require purchase of their signature Sawtooth Brewery Stein. But don’t let that dissuade you—buy the stein once and you can bring it back year after year, filling it to your heart’s delight.


Aside from brews and brats, festivalgoers have all kinds of delicious German foods to choose from, including schnitzel, landjager (bison brat), a warm Bavarian pretzel with beer cheese, and pommes frites—a hulking pile of waffle fries with beer cheese, ketchup, or fry sauce. And don’t worry; there’s plenty for the kids to enjoy too. Champions Meadow transforms into a “Bavarian playground” with bouncy houses and a face painting booth, plus kids can fill up their own steins with root beer.

Fly Fishing in The Big Wood River


Fly fishing is one of Sun Valley’s most popular outdoor activities, with an incredible variety of fishing spots for enthusiasts of all levels. The Big Wood River is a great place to set up shop for the day, and in the fall, cooler temperatures and lower water levels make for excellent wading conditions. The river’s rainbow, river, and brook trout are all very active this time of year as they prepare for winter, so you’re likely to get plenty of catches.


The river has many access points, but the best are between Ketchum and Bellevue, where there’s a mix of riffles, runs, and pools with large rainbow trout populations. More practiced anglers can also head north of Ketchum, where there’s faster pocket water. Check regulations before you wade out, as they vary depending on the section of the river, and always check stream conditions before grabbing your gear.

Wellness Retreat at the Sun Valley Spa


If days full of outdoor adventures have you wanting to unwind, look no further than the Sun Valley Spa, a rustic and serene oasis at the Sun Valley Resort. Relax with a massage, mineral bath, or nourishing skin wrap, or try out ayurvedic therapy, where reflexology pressure is applied to the hands, feet, and ears to restore natural equilibrium. You can also combat the dry autumn air with one of the spa’s hydrating facials, which can be customized to fit your skin type with a personalized booster serum.


The spa’s daily yoga classes are another perfect way to calm your mind and body, with slow, deep stretches and—in some classes—soothing sound baths that recall the whistling fall winds outside. For couples, Sun Valley Spa’s Couples Suite Experiences can turn any day into a restful and romantic getaway, with a private room, seasonal refreshments, and your choice of services.

Hiking and Biking


Sun Valley’s mountain paths are incredible all year long but are perhaps at their most stunning in the fall, when changing leaves turn the entire valley vibrant shades of yellow and orange. Over 40 miles of multi-use trails wind through the landscape, with difficulty levels ranging from calm meadow walks to steep and strenuous journeys for more experienced hikers and mountain bikers. On these paths, you’ll pass old mining sites, cabins, and bubbling creeks. The hiking trails are dog friendly, too, so make sure to bring along your best buddy.


Before you head out for a long hike or bike ride, stop by Backwoods Mountain Sports or Sturtevants for all the gear you’ll need to maximize your time outside. When you’re back from your trek, grab a bite to eat at The Kneadery, which serves up hearty, “Rocky Mountain rustic” homestyle cooking. For delicious baked goods, you can beeline it to Bigwood Bread, which has brought delicious pastries, cakes, and sandwiches to Sun Valley since 1997.

The Ernest Hemingway Memorial


The famous author held a special place in his heart for Sun Valley. He visited frequently from 1939 until his death in 1961, staying in his home along the Big Wood River. Whether you’ve read all of Hemingway’s works or know only the basics of his biography, the Hemingway Memorial is well worth a visit, especially when the forest surrounding it is aglow with fall foliage. In fact, the memorial’s inscription says of Hemingway: “Best of all he loved the fall, the leaves yellow on the cottonwoods. Leaves floating on the trout streams and above the hills. The high blue windless skies, now he will be a part of them forever.”


The bust of Hemingway, atop a simple bronze column, overlooks Sun Valley’s Trail Creek and the surrounding mountains. In front of it, a curved stone bench is the perfect place for a moment of quiet reflection—or to dive into one of Hemingway’s works with a warm cup of coffee.


Bonus: for more Hemingway artifacts, check out the Community Library, The Pioneer Saloon, and his grave site at the Ketchum Cemetery.


Trailing of the Sheep Festival


Since 1996, Sun Valley has been home to the Trailing of the Sheep Festival, a one-of-a-kind event that honors the history and culture of sheepherding in Idaho and the West at large. For five days each October, the cities of Hailey and Ketchum transform into an un-baa-lievable celebration of sheep, with activities ranging from sheepdog trials to wool dying to cheesemaking classes. The main event of the festival is the Big Sheep Parade on its final day, during which 1,200 sheep parade down Ketchum’s Main Street alongside historic sheep wagons, dancers, and ranchers.

With fewer folks in town, fall is the best time to experience this Original Mountain Town. Whether you try your hand at stein-hoisting, get lost in a Hemingway novel, or simply soak in the beauty of the changing leaves, fall is when Sun Valley’s magic truly shines, with equal parts adventure and ease.


Know Before You Go


Getting to Sun Valley, Idaho is easier than you may think. The Friedman Memorial Airport (SUN) is located 14 miles from downtown Ketchum and offers nonstop flights from six major cities including Seattle - SEA (Alaska Airlines), San Francisco - SFO (United), Los Angeles - LAX (United), Salt Lake City - SLC (Delta), Denver - DEN (United), and Chicago - ORD (United).

items.title: Why This Company is One of the Best for Finding Work
items.author: Matthew Kepnes
items.summary: Most travel is extractive and passive. You show up somewhere, take photos of the same landmarks everyone else takes photos of, eat at a restaurant the
items.text:
Most travel is extractive and passive. You show up somewhere, take photos of the same landmarks everyone else takes photos of, eat at a restaurant the guidebook recommended, and hit up some bars. You take some tours to learn about the place and, if you’re lucky, get to meet some locals on your trip. You don’t really go deep.


Even long-term travelers who talk about how they “aren’t tourists” do the same – just at a slower pace and while trying to spend less money.


And there’s nothing wrong with that. That’s just the nature of travel. While we all imagine dropping into a place, befriending locals, and having this crazy time like we’re in some movies. But that doesn’t happen. Because we’re just passing through and, for the most part, locals don’t want to become friends with tourists. In fact, most locals don’t interact with tourists. (I mean it does happen but it’s not the norm.)


If you really want a deep travel experience, you need to stay. If you want to understand a place, you need to stay. The most transformative travel experiences I’ve ever had involved contributing something and staying somewhere long enough to build real relationships. It was being embedded in a place rather than just passing through.


I think that more travelers should give back when they travel. In the old days, it was hard to find out what organizations and opportunities were legit, vetted, and actually made the lives of locals better.


Now, there’s a ton of companies that can help you not only find meaningful volunteer jobs when you travel but also paid jobs when you travel and one of the best ones is Global Work & Travel. Use code NOMADICMATT to unlock a discount on your next trip.


What Global Work & Travel Does


Global Work & Travel is the world’s largest gap year company and has been placing people on working holidays, volunteer programs, teaching positions, internships, and more for nearly 2 decades. They’ve helped over 116,000 people and they cover destinations across, the UK and Europe, the Americas, Asia, Africa, and the Pacific.


Even for experienced travelers, moving abroad can be difficult. Finding employment as a traveler, securing permanent accommodation or getting stuck in shared rooms for months on end, transport costs in a new city, interview after interview competing against locals… This is just the beginning of what long term travelers need to consider.


Fortunately, companies like Global Work & Travel provide the scaffolding or safety net that makes working abroad possible for people who don’t want to figure everything out themselves. They handle job matching, pre-departure support, visa guidance, placement, and ongoing assistance through their gWorld portal, a personal trip management app that keeps everything organized in one place. For first-timers especially, having that support structure can be the difference between actually going and endlessly deliberating. The programs they offer span a wide range:

Working Holidays – Get paid job matches in countries like Australia, Canada, UK, New Zealand, South Korea and Japan before you even leave home. Global Work & Travel also helps you set up necessary bank accounts, tax numbers, accommodation assistance, visa support and more. Duration: 4+ months. Ages 18–35 depending on nationality.


Volunteer Abroad – Work with exotic wildlife, immerse into incredible cultures, teaching, community work, construction and more across many countries. Open to ages 18–85, from as little as 1 week.


Teach Abroad – Gain an internationally recognized TEFL certification and paid job match. Included is accommodation, cultural activities, visa application support, bank and tax set up assistance to ensure everything goes smoothly. Teach English in Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, Mexico and more. Ages 18–80.


Au Pair – Become a local by living with a host family in Europe, UK, Australia, New Zealand, or North America. Accommodation, and most living expenses are usually covered.


Summer Camp – Ever seen the movie Parent Trap? Well, this is pretty much it. Work as a guide, camp counsellor or otherwise at camps in the USA, France, Canada or the UK for 3–6 months. Accommodation and meals included.


Internships – Real-world placements in international firms. Give your career a head start with specialized international work experience.

Why I Think Working Holiday Makers Are the New “Digital Nomads”


For the past decade, “digital nomad” has been the aspirational version of long term travel. Work remotely, earn in a strong currency, live somewhere cheaper, repeat.


But that model only really works for a small subset of people. You need a remote job, a certain income level, and often a level of career stability that most younger travelers simply don’t have yet.


Working holidays flip that.


Instead of bringing a job with you, you get one when you arrive. You integrate into the local economy instead of floating above it. You meet people through work, not just coworking spaces or short-term hostels. And you build a life somewhere, not just a temporary routine.


In a lot of ways, working holiday makers are having a more grounded and accessible version of what people think digital nomad life is. You’re not just passing through, you’re actually living there. You have coworkers, a schedule, a reason to stay longer than a week, and a chance to build real lifetime connections.


It’s also far more realistic for most people. You don’t need a remote business or years of experience. You just need the willingness to go and the right setup to make it happen.


That’s why I think we’re seeing a shift. Less “how do I work remotely?” and more “how do I actually live and work abroad for a year?”


And that’s exactly where structured programs like Global Work & Travel come in. They remove the biggest barriers, finding a job, navigating visas, getting set up, so people can actually make that shift from idea to reality.


For a lot of travelers, this isn’t just an alternative to digital nomad life. It’s a more sustainable, accessible, and realistic way to actually live and work abroad.


Why I think Volunteering Matters


Volunteering abroad has a complicated reputation, and it’s worth being honest about that. There are lots of bad volunteer programs out there in the world. Programs that don’t really give back and are designed to make travelers “feel” like they did something but really are just profit driven campaigns. Global Work & Travel’s vets programs in the areas such as wildlife conservation, community development, education, and healthcare in the locations and countries it operates so you know the program you sign up for is legit.


The case for ethical, well-structured volunteering is genuinely strong. When you work alongside local Zanzibar communities on problems they’ve defined as priorities, or with wildlife and conservation in South Africa or Elephant rehabilitation in Thailand — something shifts in how you understand the world. Not only are you helping to give back to a place but you also understand the true needs of a the people and ecosystems living there, but also helping overcome the struggles they go through. It opens your mind and shifts your perspective.


Their Global Animal Welfare Fund also channels resources directly into conservation projects at their partner sites, so the impact extends beyond individual placements.


What I Love About Working Holidays


Working holidays let you truly experience a country instead of just visiting it. You immerse yourself in the culture by living like a local every day. You meet more people both locals and fellow travellers while building real friendships. Best of all, you get paid to travel, so you can stay much longer instead of rushing through in a few weeks. This lets you experience local life deeply, discover hidden spots, and understand how people really live in different places. You also build valuable skills, boost your resume with international experience, and make long-term travel more affordable since your income covers the costs. Plus, you gain a real cultural understanding that no short holiday can match. All that while stil getting paid? Not bad right?!


Working holidays turn travel into a true lifestyle, not just another 2 week vacation.


What I Like About How Global Work & Travel Operates


Global Work & Travel are the world leaders in long term travel and offer a ton of options for travelers looking to volunteer, work, or spend extended time in a destination. Some things I like about them.

Their lifetime deposit policy is genuinely unusual: if your plans change, your deposit doesn’t disappear. It stays on your account indefinitely and can be transferred to a different program or destination


The gWorld portal is genuinely useful. This pre-departure tool that helps you with your visa application, access exclusive deals, connect with others on your program, and even begin language learning before you arrive.


They have transparent 24/5 worldwide human support. When something goes wrong abroad, being able to reach a human in local time is worth more than any amount of pre-trip planning.


With over 619k followers on Instagram, it’s easy to connect with and make friends with people before you go.


A structured start to your trip is the best way to save money, time and stress. The Global network and support are there to help and guide you from start to finish. Use code NOMADICMATT for a discount on your trip.

Frequently Asked Questions


Do I need prior experience to work abroad with Global Work & Travel? For most trips, generally nothing more than basic work experience is required. Teaching programs include TEFL training, and volunteering can be started from no experience.


What’s the minimum age? Most programs are open from age 18. Working holiday visas typically cap at 35 depending on the destination country but volunteer and teach programs are open to ages 18–80.


How long does the whole process take? It varies by programs and destination. Most people book their trips 6-12 months in advance for proper planning, job matching and visa quotas. You can get started for as little as $1 here.


Is my money safe if things change? Global Work & Travel and their lifetime deposit policy means your initial payment doesn’t expire. They are also members of many consumer protection services to further support travelers.


Can I go as a solo traveler? Yes, and this is actually one of the most common scenarios. The gWorld Community and programs group connections mean you’ll be meeting others in the same position quickly.


***


Travel has always been best when it’s been more than tourism. The moments that stay with you — that you actually tell people about five years later — are never the ones where you queued to see a famous landmark. They’re the ones where you connect with people. They are the moments where you did something.


Global Work & Travel makes doing something deep accessible in a way that genuinely wasn’t available a decade ago. If you’ve been thinking about doing something like this but the logistics have felt too complicated, check them out and use code NOMADICMATT to unlock a $100 discount on your trip.


How to Travel the World on $75 a Day

My New York Times best-selling book to travel will teach you how to master the art of travel so that you’ll get off save money, always find deals, and have a deeper travel experience. It’s your A to Z planning guide that the BBC called the “bible for budget travelers.”


Click here to learn more and start reading it today!


Book Your Trip: Logistical Tips and Tricks


Book Your Flight

Find a cheap flight by using Skyscanner. It’s my favorite search engine because it searches websites and airlines around the globe so you always know no stone is being left unturned.


Book Your Accommodation

You can book your hostel with Hostelworld. If you want to stay somewhere other than a hostel, use Booking.com as it consistently returns the cheapest rates for guesthouses and hotels.


Don’t Forget Travel Insurance

Travel insurance will protect you against illness, injury, theft, and cancellations. It’s comprehensive protection in case anything goes wrong. I never go on a trip without it as I’ve had to use it many times in the past. My favorite companies that offer the best service and value are:

SafetyWing (best for budget travelers)


World Nomads (best for mid-range travelers)


InsureMyTrip (for those 70 and over)


Medjet (for additional evacuation coverage)

Want to Travel for Free?

Travel credit cards allow you to earn points that can be redeemed for free flights and accommodation — all without any extra spending. Check out my guide to picking the right card and my current favorites to get started and see the latest best deals.


Need a Rental Car?

Discover Cars is a budget-friendly international car rental website. No matter where you’re headed, they’ll be able to find the best — and cheapest — rental for your trip!


Need Help Finding Activities for Your Trip?

Get Your Guide is a huge online marketplace where you can find cool walking tours, fun excursions, skip-the-line tickets, private guides, and more.


Ready to Book Your Trip?

Check out my resource page for the best companies to use when you travel. I list all the ones I use when I travel. They are the best in class and you can’t go wrong using them on your trip.

Now, there’s a ton of companies that can help you not only find meaningful volunteer jobs when you travel but also paid jobs when you travel and one of the best ones is Global Work & Travel. Use code NOMADICMATT to unlock a discount on your next trip.
What Global Work & Travel Does

Global Work & Travel is the world’s largest gap year company and has been placing people on working holidays, volunteer programs, teaching positions, internships, and more for nearly 2 decades. They’ve helped over 116,000 people and they cover destinations across, the UK and Europe, the Americas, Asia, Africa, and the Pacific.

Even for experienced travelers, moving abroad can be difficult. Finding employment as a traveler, securing permanent accommodation or getting stuck in shared rooms for months on end, transport costs in a new city, interview after interview competing against locals… This is just the beginning of what long term travelers need to consider.

Fortunately, companies like Global Work & Travel provide the scaffolding or safety net that makes working abroad possible for people who don’t want to figure everything out themselves. They handle job matching, pre-departure support, visa guidance, placement, and ongoing assistance through their gWorld portal, a personal trip management app that keeps everything organized in one place. For first-timers especially, having that support structure can be the difference between actually going and endlessly deliberating. The programs they offer span a wide range:

Working Holidays – Get paid job matches in countries like Australia, Canada, UK, New Zealand, South Korea and Japan before you even leave home. Global Work & Travel also helps you set up necessary bank accounts, tax numbers, accommodation assistance, visa support and more. Duration: 4+ months. Ages 18–35 depending on nationality.
Volunteer Abroad – Work with exotic wildlife, immerse into incredible cultures, teaching, community work, construction and more across many countries. Open to ages 18–85, from as little as 1 week.

Teach Abroad – Gain an internationally recognized TEFL certification and paid job match. Included is accommodation, cultural activities, visa application support, bank and tax set up assistance to ensure everything goes smoothly. Teach English in Thailand, Vietnam, Japan, Mexico and more. Ages 18–80.
Au Pair – Become a local by living with a host family in Europe, UK, Australia, New Zealand, or North America. Accommodation, and most living expenses are usually covered.

Summer Camp – Ever seen the movie Parent Trap? Well, this is pretty much it. Work as a guide, camp counsellor or otherwise at camps in the USA, France, Canada or the UK for 3–6 months. Accommodation and meals included.
Internships – Real-world placements in international firms. Give your career a head start with specialized international work experience.
Why I Think Working Holiday Makers Are the New “Digital Nomads”
For the past decade, “digital nomad” has been the aspirational version of long term travel. Work remotely, earn in a strong currency, live somewhere cheaper, repeat.
But that model only really works for a small subset of people. You need a remote job, a certain income level, and often a level of career stability that most younger travelers simply don’t have yet.
Working holidays flip that.

Instead of bringing a job with you, you get one when you arrive. You integrate into the local economy instead of floating above it. You meet people through work, not just coworking spaces or short-term hostels. And you build a life somewhere, not just a temporary routine.

In a lot of ways, working holiday makers are having a more grounded and accessible version of what people think digital nomad life is. You’re not just passing through, you’re actually living there. You have coworkers, a schedule, a reason to stay longer than a week, and a chance to build real lifetime connections.
It’s also far more realistic for most people. You don’t need a remote business or years of experience. You just need the willingness to go and the right setup to make it happen.
That’s why I think we’re seeing a shift. Less “how do I work remotely?” and more “how do I actually live and work abroad for a year?”

And that’s exactly where structured programs like Global Work & Travel come in. They remove the biggest barriers, finding a job, navigating visas, getting set up, so people can actually make that shift from idea to reality.
For a lot of travelers, this isn’t just an alternative to digital nomad life. It’s a more sustainable, accessible, and realistic way to actually live and work abroad.
Why I think Volunteering Matters

Volunteering abroad has a complicated reputation, and it’s worth being honest about that. There are lots of bad volunteer programs out there in the world. Programs that don’t really give back and are designed to make travelers “feel” like they did something but really are just profit driven campaigns. Global Work & Travel’s vets programs in the areas such as wildlife conservation, community development, education, and healthcare in the locations and countries it operates so you know the program you sign up for is legit.

The case for ethical, well-structured volunteering is genuinely strong. When you work alongside local Zanzibar communities on problems they’ve defined as priorities, or with wildlife and conservation in South Africa or Elephant rehabilitation in Thailand — something shifts in how you understand the world. Not only are you helping to give back to a place but you also understand the true needs of a the people and ecosystems living there, but also helping overcome the struggles they go through. It opens your mind and shifts your perspective.
Their Global Animal Welfare Fund also channels resources directly into conservation projects at their partner sites, so the impact extends beyond individual placements.
What I Love About Working Holidays

Working holidays let you truly experience a country instead of just visiting it. You immerse yourself in the culture by living like a local every day. You meet more people both locals and fellow travellers while building real friendships. Best of all, you get paid to travel, so you can stay much longer instead of rushing through in a few weeks. This lets you experience local life deeply, discover hidden spots, and understand how people really live in different places. You also build valuable skills, boost your resume with international experience, and make long-term travel more affordable since your income covers the costs. Plus, you gain a real cultural understanding that no short holiday can match. All that while stil getting paid? Not bad right?!
Working holidays turn travel into a true lifestyle, not just another 2 week vacation.
What I Like About How Global Work & Travel Operates

Global Work & Travel are the world leaders in long term travel and offer a ton of options for travelers looking to volunteer, work, or spend extended time in a destination. Some things I like about them.

Their lifetime deposit policy is genuinely unusual: if your plans change, your deposit doesn’t disappear. It stays on your account indefinitely and can be transferred to a different program or destination

The gWorld portal is genuinely useful. This pre-departure tool that helps you with your visa application, access exclusive deals, connect with others on your program, and even begin language learning before you arrive.
They have transparent 24/5 worldwide human support. When something goes wrong abroad, being able to reach a human in local time is worth more than any amount of pre-trip planning.
With over 619k followers on Instagram, it’s easy to connect with and make friends with people before you go.

Do I need prior experience to work abroad with Global Work & Travel? For most trips, generally nothing more than basic work experience is required. Teaching programs include TEFL training, and volunteering can be started from no experience.
What’s the minimum age? Most programs are open from age 18. Working holiday visas typically cap at 35 depending on the destination country but volunteer and teach programs are open to ages 18–80.

How long does the whole process take? It varies by programs and destination. Most people book their trips 6-12 months in advance for proper planning, job matching and visa quotas. You can get started for as little as $1 here.

Is my money safe if things change? Global Work & Travel and their lifetime deposit policy means your initial payment doesn’t expire. They are also members of many consumer protection services to further support travelers.

Can I go as a solo traveler? Yes, and this is actually one of the most common scenarios. The gWorld Community and programs group connections mean you’ll be meeting others in the same position quickly.

Travel has always been best when it’s been more than tourism. The moments that stay with you — that you actually tell people about five years later — are never the ones where you queued to see a famous landmark. They’re the ones where you connect with people. They are the moments where you did something.

Global Work & Travel makes doing something deep accessible in a way that genuinely wasn’t available a decade ago. If you’ve been thinking about doing something like this but the logistics have felt too complicated, check them out and use code NOMADICMATT to unlock a $100 discount on your trip.

items.text:
This year has been one of the most important, yet challenging years of my life. And as we’ll see, that might not be a coincidence.


As you probably know, I’ve been calling out some of the shady dealings and worst practices of the self-help industry for my entire career. Whether it’s slimy sales tactics, unrealistic and unscientific advice, or promising results that simply aren’t possible, I’ve dedicated much of my adult life to “cleaning up” this space as much as possible.


You could even say that I have come to see this as my purpose, my calling in life.


About a year ago, a number of people I know started asking me about using ChatGPT as a therapist or life coach. Turns out, millions of people were doing this.


I was intrigued, so I tried it out. The results were… mixed.


Very mixed.


On the one hand, AI has access to all of the known psychological research, is trained on thousands of hours of clinical transcripts and possesses pretty much all of human knowledge within it.


On the other hand, it often has no clue how to use it.


ChatGPT, in particular, seemed to just want to validate me, tell me how great I was, reinforce any bad beliefs I might have had, and avoid saying anything uncomfortable.


This, I saw, was a huge problem.


So, I started researching how to train an AI to challenge you, to look at your underlying motivations and values and adapt to your personality. This led me down a rabbit hole, as I studied prompt engineering, LLM models and eval systems. I built AI agents, pitted them against each other, and organized them into “councils.”


I got so into it, that I eventually began talking to professional AI engineers, technical geniuses who have built AI systems that have been used by tens of millions of people. Pretty soon, we found ourselves working together. They too, saw the problem and were energized by the mission.


So, at the beginning of this year, we started an AI company. And this was either the smartest or stupidest thing I’ve ever done. I poured all of my extra time, energy, and not to mention my own money into it. All year, I worked nights and weekends, skipped vacations, ditched friends and family, sacrificing health, relationships and sleep to get it over the line.


And this is the paradox of purpose: you give up so much… yet, it somehow feels worth it.


We like to imagine that living with purpose is fun or euphoric. That we wake up every day with a smile on our face, even before the caffeine hits.


That’s bullshit. Because when you believe in something, when you become obsessed with something, you sacrifice yourself to it. And that sacrifice actually feels like pain and stress and doubt. Not fun.


Oh, that’s the name of the AI we built, by the way… Purpose.


It is an AI designed to go deep, to understand your values and needs within minutes, to be there at all times of the day (or night), to push you to be better, to challenge your assumptions, to point out your blindspots, and to compassionately nudge you back into alignment with what you really care about.


In short, we built it not to make you feel good, but to help you find a greater purpose.


And I’m extremely proud of it. I do not exaggerate when I say it may be the best thing I’ve ever done… but only time will tell.


I would love for you to try it. It is free to sign up and use it. We have a free personality assessment that you can take where the AI reads your soul within a few minutes of meeting you, and then if you want to continue the conversation we have a free trial period.

items.title: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You
items.author: Rebecca Firkser
items.summary: Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser
items.text:
Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week.

While you can’t scroll through a healthy-recipe collection without seeing a sweet potato or three, you’d be hard-pressed to find white potatoes like russets included on most lists. These spuds are often seen as bad for you, while their orange-hued brethren have taken on a health halo. But why? When you look at the nutrition facts, the two are nearly identical.

“Diets like keto and Atkins, and the recent TikTok protein craze can promote the idea that carbs drive weight gain or that they provide empty calories,” says Hannah Sorrell, a registered dietitian at Alike Nutrition. “However, carbohydrates are our brain and body’s main fuel source.” What’s more, Sorrell notes that carbs are also the only macronutrient that contain fiber (a large russet brings about four grams if eaten skin-on).

Energy-boosting carbohydrates like potatoes prove especially valuable to those who exercise vigorously. Ever sucked down a gel during a run or chugged coconut water after a tough workout? That boost of energy comes from carbs. While many active adults pat themselves on the back as they munch on a salad post–Barry’s Bootcamp, proper fuel and recovery can be much less green.

My new recipe is basically the opposite of a salad. It’s a big fat potato, smothered in saucy, spicy ground beef. And yeah, it’s for my column on healthy cooking.

Especially for high-intensity workouts, “fueling with carbs is the key to success,” says Julie Jefferson, a Brooklyn-based trainer and HYROX coach. Jefferson—who adds she’s been known to eat a slice of pizza before a run—says a big mistake she sees people make is underfueling. “White potatoes provide an easy way to increase carb intake. And because they are also an easy food to digest, they can help training and recovery feel easier on our bodies.”

But carbs—and protein and fat—are necessary for moderately active folks as well. You don’t need to be a marathoner to earn a filling dinner. You just need to be a human. That’s it.

We can point a finger at diet culture and careful marketing for the way that a rotating cast of foods have been characterized as “good” or “bad” over the years. Like carbs, red meat has had its own contentious journey in the spotlight. One minute, it’s an important source of protein, rich in iron, zinc, and vitamin B; the next, it’s high in saturated fat that can increase risk of heart disease and cancer. Technically, all true!

In addition to being lauded in the updated dietary guidelines from the Department of Health and Human Services (which has received mixed reactions from nutrition experts), meat is having a moment in the fitness community. Specifically, lean ground beef for its protein-to-fat breakdown. “Boy kibble,” or some slop of mince and carbs, has become the new hyperfixation dinner for many active adults (of all genders) for performance and recovery.

It’s quick, budget-friendly, and not all that different from this dressed-up potato. Of course, I’d like to think this recipe is far too nice-looking to ever be associated with pup chow, but we all know beauty is in the eye of the beholder.

Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

This picadillo-inspired topping would taste good on a shoe.

items.title: Japan’s Nuclear Power Plants in 2026
items.summary: TEPCO’s restart at its Kashiwazaki-Kariwa Nuclear Power Station in 2026 brought the total number of reactors restarted across the country since the 2011 Great
items.text:
TEPCO’s restart at its Kashiwazaki-Kariwa Nuclear Power Station in 2026 brought the total number of reactors restarted across the country since the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake to 15.

Hamaoka Withdraws Restart Application

Due to expectations of increased electricity demand driven by the construction of generative AI data centers, the Japanese government’s February 2025 basic energy plan stated that it would make maximum use of the country’s existing nuclear power plants. In July 2026, it announced a policy to replace two to five nuclear reactors by the 2040s.

In January 2026, Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO) restarted the number 6 reactor at its Kashiwazaki-Kariwa Nuclear Power Station in Niigata Prefecture for the first time in nearly 14 years, while Hokkaidō Electric Power is expected to bring its Tomari Nuclear Power Station back online in 2027.

Amid these developments, it came to light in January 2026 that Chūbu Electric Power had falsified data concerning earthquake resistance at its Hamaoka Nuclear Power Station in Shizuoka Prefecture. On September 14, the company announced the resignations of President Hayashi Kingo and Chairman Katsuno Satoru, as well as the withdrawal of its application for safety review to restart Hamaoka’s number 3 and number 4 reactors. In addition to making prospects for restarts uncertain, the scandal has rekindled public anxiety and distrust over nuclear power, in a setback to the government’s energy policy.

Nuclear Power Plants: Major Developments Since the Great East Japan Earthquake

September 2026 Chūbu Electric Power withdraws its application to restart reactors at its Hamaoka Nuclear Power Station in Shizuoka Prefecture.

July 2026 The Nuclear Regulation Authority announces that Chūbu Electric Power attempted to cover up evidence after the start of an investigation into seismic resistance tests at its Hamaoka Nuclear Power Station.

January 2026 TEPCO restarts the number 6 reactor at its Kashiwazaki-Kariwa Nuclear Power Station in Niigata Prefecture for the first time in 13 years and 10 months. This is the first restart for a reactor operated by TEPCO since the Great East Japan Earthquake in March 2011.

January 2026 Chūbū Electric Power announces that it may have underestimated expected seismic movement during safety reviews required for the restart of its Hamaoka Nuclear Power Station.

December 2025 Hokkaidō Governor Suzuki Naomichi approves the restart of Hokkaidō Electric Power’s Tomari Nuclear Power Station, with operations expected to resume in early 2027.

November 2025 Niigata Governor Hanazumi Hideyo approves the restart of TEPCO’s Kashiwazaki-Kariwa Nuclear Power Station, which is expected to resume operation within the fiscal year, at earliest. It will become the first active TEPCO nuclear plant since the 2011 Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident.

February 2025 The government approves a new basic energy plan. This removes a phrase about minimizing dependence on nuclear power, which had been in the document since 2014, instead stating an intention to make the maximum use of existing plants.

December 2024 The number 2 reactor at Shimane Nuclear Power Station (Chūgoku Electric Power Company) resumes operation.

October 2024 The number 2 reactor at Onagawa Nuclear Power Station (Tōhoku Electric Power Company) resumes operation. It is the first plant in eastern Japan to restart after the 2011 Great Eastern Japan Earthquake.

October 2024 The Nuclear Regulation Authority approves Kansai Electric Power Company’s plans to continue operating Takahama Nuclear Power Station in Fukui Prefecture, Japan’s oldest nuclear plant, which will have been in use for 50 years in November 2024. It is the first time for a plant more than 50 years old to receive approval to operate under the present system.

September 2023 Restart of the number 2 reactor at Takahama Nuclear Power Station (Kansai Electric Power Company).

August 2023 Start of the release of treated water containing radioactive tritium that had accumulated at the number 1 reactor of Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station.

July 2023 The number 1 reactor at Takahama Nuclear Power Station resumes operation after a 12-year hiatus.

May 2023 The GX Decarbonization Power Supply bill is enacted. In order to ensure stable power supply and achieve decarbonization, significant changes are made to the safety regulations stipulating that the operating period for reactors is “40 years in principle and a maximum of 60 years,” making it possible for them to operate for periods of longer than 60 years.

June 2021 Mihama Nuclear Power Station (Kansai Electric Power Company) restarts operation for the first time since being shut down for routine inspection a decade before. At 44 years since it began operation, it is the first nuclear plant to restart despite being more than 40 years old.

July 2018 The cabinet approves the fifth energy basic plan, with the intention to have nuclear power account for 20%–22% of power generation in 2030.

March/June 2018 The number 3 and number 4 reactors at Genkai Nuclear Power Station (Kyūshū Electric Power Company) resume operation.

March/May 2018 The number 3 and number 4 reactors at Ōi Nuclear Power Station resume operation.

August 2016 The number 3 reactor at Ikata Nuclear Power Station (Shikoku Electric Power Company) resumes operation.

January/February 2016 The number 3 and number 4 reactors at Takahama Nuclear Power Station (Kansai Electric Power Company) resume operation.

August/October 2015 The number 1 and number 2 reactors at Sendai Nuclear Power Station (Kyūshū Electric Power Company) resume operation. These are the first restarts since the introduction of the new standards and follow almost two years without nuclear power in Japan.

April 2014 The cabinet approves the fourth energy basic plan, positioning nuclear power plants as an important base-load power source, while also pledging to reduce dependency on nuclear power as much as possible by introducing renewable energy.

July 2013 New regulatory standards relating to natural disasters and terrorist attacks introduced for nuclear power plants.

September 2012 Nuclear Regulation Authority established.

July 2012 The number 3 and number 4 reactors at Ōi Nuclear Power Station (Kansai Electric Power Company) resume operation, ending a 2-month period of no nuclear power generation in Japan.

June 2012 The operating period of nuclear power plants is limited to 40 years in principle.

May 2012 Tomari Nuclear Power Station (Hokkaidō Electric Power Company) suspends operation of its number 3 reactor. For the first time in 42 years there are no nuclear power plants operating within Japan.

March 2011 The Great East Japan Earthquake and TEPCO Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station accident take place.

In January 2026, Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO) restarted the number 6 reactor at its Kashiwazaki-Kariwa Nuclear Power Station in Niigata Prefecture for the first time in nearly 14 years, while Hokkaidō Electric Power is expected to bring its Tomari Nuclear Power Station back online in 2027.

Amid these developments, it came to light in January 2026 that Chūbu Electric Power had falsified data concerning earthquake resistance at its Hamaoka Nuclear Power Station in Shizuoka Prefecture. On September 14, the company announced the resignations of President Hayashi Kingo and Chairman Katsuno Satoru, as well as the withdrawal of its application for safety review to restart Hamaoka’s number 3 and number 4 reactors. In addition to making prospects for restarts uncertain, the scandal has rekindled public anxiety and distrust over nuclear power, in a setback to the government’s energy policy.

items.title: Atlanta Is the New Bagel Capital of the South
items.author: Sheeka Sanahori
items.summary:
Atlanta has historically favored biscuits. But recently, the southern capital city has embraced a northern import: New York City-style bagels.

Emerald City
items.text:
Atlanta has historically favored biscuits. But recently, the southern capital city has embraced a northern import: New York City-style bagels.

Emerald City Bagels, which originally opened in 2018 in East Atlanta Village, doesn’t represent an NYC borough by name, but the mother-daughter owners, Deanna and Jackie Halcrow, are unmistakenly Long Islanders. The original location and new store on Atlanta’s Beltline drip in retro New York deli style: Green and white subway tile line the walls, while staff don paper soda jerk hats and white aprons. They stuff everything bagels schmeared with green olive cream cheese into paper bags as customers take their orders to go.

Emerald City isn’t alone in its love of NYC foods: in the suburb of Stone Mountain, NY Deli & Juice Bar recently began serving chopped cheese sandwiches in a building that had once been a Waffle House. The customary counter and high chairs that once held pecan waffles and smothered hash browns have been replaced with a long bodega-style service counter.

New York imports have been flooding Atlanta—from pizza to Chinese to chopped cheese—but bagels are the most prominent addition to the city’s food scene, a reflection of a North-to-South migration in the last few years.

Why the Best Bagels in the US Aren’t All in New York Anymore

From San Francisco to Philly and beyond, regional bagel culture is drawing intense obsession—and very long lines.

New Yorkers are Moving South

“This is comfort food, a taste of home,” said Julie Dragich, part-owner of The Bronx Bagel Buggy. “I think many of our New York customers feel the same way.”

Those customers are easy to come by in Atlanta, according to the U.S. Census data. More than 50,000 New Yorkers moved to Georgia from 2021-2024; they moved to Georgia at similar rates of people making regional moves, such as from Alabama or South Carolina to Georgia. According to the Atlanta Regional Commission, most young adults moving to Atlanta from out of state are relocating from New York City.

There are a few reasons New Yorkers have been moving to metro-Atlanta, including milder winters and job opportunities. But across the board, many New Yorkers cite a better cost of living as the top catalyst for the southern migration.

“A house that's $300,000, $400,000 in Georgia would be over a million dollars in New York,” said Kamal Dorsainville, who’s originally from Brooklyn.

His wife, Susan Dorsainville, said when they showed friends Georgia’s housing prices, their reaction was swift–we’re coming too. “And then they brought two more families down with them,” she said.

Andrew Thomas Lee

Getting the Flavors Right

When the couple flew back home for work or family visits, their fellow New York transplants requested they bring back bagels, enough to fill up suitcases, so they opened SDK'S Cafe and Coffee to meet the demand. The coffee shop ships New York bagels from a national distributor two to three times a week so New Yorkers can get a taste of home. (The couple did not disclose their supplier.)

Steven Novotny, Dragich’s partner in The Bronx Bagel Buggy, grew up in the restaurant business. His family owned delicatessens in the Bronx, but it took him and Dragich months to teach themselves the art of New York bagel-making. They started from scratch—first, with a class run by King Arthur Baking that explained the basics—measuring dough, baking time, and perfecting flavors. A few months in, they knew they had a good product because they’d sell out of their bagels within the hour at the Brookhaven Farmers Market.

Welcome to the Great Bagel Boom

For too long, bagels have been just average outside NYC. But now, absolutely superb versions are having a national moment from California to Florida—and they're worth waiting in line to try.

It would take them three more years to feel ready enough to open their brick and mortar shop. Before taking the plunge, they talked to established NYC bagel shop owners and equipment manufacturer Empire Baking Company to learn more about large scale production. When they were ready, they took a four-day trip back home. Every stop on the trip–to shops like Utopia Bagel in Queens–was to prepare them to open an authentic New York shop in the heart of the South.

The stakes are high because as soon as New Yorkers step inside the Chamblee shop, they announce, first, that they’re from New York, and next, that they’re skeptical about Atlanta having the real deal. “I kept thinking maybe I'm going to put my birth certificate on the wall, on a big frame to show, hey, this is the truth,” Novotny said.

For Dragich, New York water isn’t necessary for an authentic flavor. The ingredients they leave out of their recipe is more important than what they put in. They don’t add sugar or dough additives to make dough last longer. The key is in rolling dough by hand and giving it plenty of time to ferment.

After New Yorkers bite through the crunchy outer layer into the soft dough inside, they relax, and even return with their fellow transplants.

On the other hand, there’s a learning curve for born-and-raised Atlanta bagel customers, unfamiliar with NYC’s bagel rituals.

“We were both trying to teach people how to eat a bagel without toasting it, because truly you're not supposed to toast a bagel,” said Deanna Halcrow, recalling her early years taking orders at Emerald City Bagels. Her daughter called it a “Herculean task,” giving away a ton of untoasted bagel sandwiches to convert Southerners to eat bagels the New York way.

Even though Atlantans may be uninitiated to the rules of eating a New York bagel, many welcome the sudden addition of the northern cuisine.

“I would love to see more New York staples come down here,” says Jasmin Moore, a born-and-raised Georgian. She still prefers Southern biscuits over a bagel, but treasures having Brooklyn Bagel & Deli in her neighborhood for variety. “I don’t feel like any restaurants that come from out of town are pushing out anything local that has good flavor.”

Atlanta food historian Akila McConnell says Atlanta’s welcoming attitude to new cuisines is because the city was built on immigrant flavors. Even with its own food traditions, Atlanta has historically made room for New York flavors. In the late 19th century, Atlanta followed New York’s love of oysters.

Perhaps the New York bagel purists will convince Atlantans to embrace the soft interior and chewy exterior of an untoasted New York bagel. Or maybe they’ll embrace something new. No matter what, it’s a heartwarming cultural exchange for Kamal Dorsainville.

“Now they’re part of the family,” he declared. “With a different accent.”
